arc.en.arc1.title: Foundations
cando.en.a0.u01.greet: Can say hello, thank you, please, sorry, and goodbye in everyday moments.
cando.en.a0.u02.sounds: Can hear and copy the core vowel and consonant contrasts of English.
cando.en.a0.u01.basics: Can use a handful of rescue phrases: greetings, thanks, and asking people to slow down.
cando.en.a0.u01.numbers: Can say and understand the numbers from one to ten.
cando.en.a1.u01.greet: Can greet people, respond to greetings, and say goodbye politely.
cando.en.a1.u01.intro-self: Can give their name and introduce themselves with a simple sentence.
cando.en.a1.u02.langs: Can say which languages they speak.
cando.en.a1.u02.origin: Can say which country they are from and ask others the same.
cando.en.a1.u03.family: Can name close family members and say simple things about them.
cando.en.a1.u04.count: Can count, say prices and ages, and catch numbers when they hear them.
cando.en.a1.u05.clock: Can ask for and give the time in simple terms.
cando.en.a1.u05.dates: Can say the day, the date, and when something happens.
cando.en.a1.u06.likes: Can say what food and drink they like and want.
cando.en.a1.u07.order: Can order food and drink politely and ask for the bill.
cando.en.a1.u08.around-town: Can say what there is in their town and where things are.
cando.en.a1.u09.routine: Can describe their daily routine and how often they do things.
cando.en.a1.u10.jobs: Can say what they do for work and ask others about their job.
cando.en.a1.u11.possessions: Can say what they have and ask what others have.
cando.en.a1.u12.describe-things: Can name colors and clothes and describe what things look like.
cando.en.a1.u13.ability: Can say what they can and can't do and make simple requests.
cando.en.a1.u14.now: Can describe what is happening around them at this moment.
cando.en.a1.u15.weather: Can talk about the weather and the seasons in simple terms.
cando.en.a1.u16.transport: Can buy tickets, follow simple directions, and use public transport.
cando.en.a1.u17.prices: Can ask how much things cost and handle simple purchases.
cando.en.a1.u18.describe-people: Can describe what people look like and what they are like.
cando.en.a1.u19.hobbies: Can talk about hobbies and free-time activities they enjoy.
cando.en.a1.u20.past: Can say where they were and what they did in simple past sentences.
cando.en.a1.u21.tell-past: Can tell a short story about last week using common past verbs.
cando.en.a1.u22.plans: Can talk about plans and invite people to do things together.
cando.en.a1.u23.feelings: Can say how they feel and describe simple health problems.
cando.en.a1.u24.home: Can describe their home and the rooms and things in it.
cando.en.a1.u25.compare: Can compare people, places, and things in simple sentences.
cando.en.a1.u26.connect: Can join simple ideas with and, but, and because.
cando.en.a1.u27.about-me: Can give a short spoken introduction: who they are, what they do, and what they like.
cando.en.a1.u28.show: Can put the whole arc together in one review session.
gn.en.gn.adv-freq.note: Words like usually, often, and sometimes say how frequent a habit is. They go before the main verb and after be: "I usually walk. She is often late."
gn.en.gn.adv-freq.title: Adverbs of frequency
gn.en.gn.art-the.note: "The" means the one we both know: "the station", "the sun", or the second mention. General plurals drop it: "I like dogs."
gn.en.gn.art-the.title: the (basic)
gn.en.gn.articles-a-an.note: Use "a" before consonant sounds and "an" before vowel sounds: a book, an apple, an hour. It marks one, non-specific thing.
gn.en.gn.articles-a-an.title: a / an
gn.en.gn.be-1sg-2sg.note: "Am" goes with I, and "are" goes with you: "I am Anna. You are my friend." These two forms carry your first introductions.
gn.en.gn.be-1sg-2sg.title: be: I am / you are
gn.en.gn.be-all.note: Am, is, and are across all persons: he, she, and it take "is"; we, you, and they take "are". "She is a doctor. They are from Peru."
gn.en.gn.be-all.title: be: the full present
gn.en.gn.be-neg.note: Add "not" after be: "I am not tired. She isn't here." The short forms isn't and aren't sound most natural in speech.
gn.en.gn.be-neg.title: be: negation
gn.en.gn.be-yesno-q.note: Flip be to the front: "You are tired." becomes "Are you tired?" The word order alone makes it a question — no extra word is needed.
gn.en.gn.be-yesno-q.title: Yes/no questions with be
gn.en.gn.can-ability.note: "I can swim. He can't drive." One form for every person, and the verb after it stays bare.
gn.en.gn.can-ability.title: can / can't (ability)
gn.en.gn.can-request.note: "Can I have the menu? Can you help me?" — the everyday polite ask, for both permission and favors.
gn.en.gn.can-request.title: can (requests)
gn.en.gn.comp-superl.note: Short adjectives take -er and -est (older, the oldest); long ones use more and most. Good becomes better and best. Compare with "than": "My city is bigger than yours."
gn.en.gn.comp-superl.title: Comparatives & superlatives
gn.en.gn.conn-basic.note: Join ideas: "I like tea and coffee. It's small but nice. I stayed home because I was tired."
gn.en.gn.conn-basic.title: and / but / because
gn.en.gn.dem-sg.note: "This" points to something near you and "that" to something farther away: "This is my phone. That is your bag."
gn.en.gn.dem-sg.title: this / that
gn.en.gn.do-neg.note: "I don't know. She doesn't eat meat." Don't or doesn't plus the bare verb — the -s moves onto "does" and leaves the verb.
gn.en.gn.do-neg.title: Negatives with don't/doesn't
gn.en.gn.do-quest.note: "Do you like tea? Does she work here?" Do or does starts the question and the main verb stays in its base form.
gn.en.gn.do-quest.title: Questions with do/does
gn.en.gn.dummy-it.note: English needs a subject even for weather and time: "It is raining. It's cold. It's late." The "it" points at nothing — it just fills the subject seat.
gn.en.gn.dummy-it.title: it for weather & time
gn.en.gn.going-to.note: Be plus going to plus a verb for plans: "I'm going to visit my aunt tomorrow. We're going to travel in June."
gn.en.gn.going-to.title: going to (plans)
gn.en.gn.have-got.note: Possession: "I have two brothers. She has a car." You may also hear "have got" — treat it as the same meaning.
gn.en.gn.have-got.title: have / has
gn.en.gn.how-much-many.note: "How many" with countable things ("How many apples?") and "how much" with uncountable ones ("How much water?"). Prices use "How much is it?"
gn.en.gn.how-much-many.title: How much / How many
gn.en.gn.imperatives.note: Tell someone what to do with the bare verb: "Turn left. Wait here. Please don't stop." Adding "please" keeps it friendly.
gn.en.gn.imperatives.title: Imperatives
gn.en.gn.like-want-noun.note: Verb plus thing, nothing in between: "I like coffee. I want water." The person doing the liking is the subject.
gn.en.gn.like-want-noun.title: like / want + noun
gn.en.gn.numbers-1-100.note: Count to one hundred and watch the -teen versus -ty trap: thirteen and thirty sound close, so the stress tells them apart.
gn.en.gn.numbers-1-100.title: Numbers 1–100
gn.en.gn.obj-pron.note: Me, you, him, her, it, us, them — they come after the verb: "Call me. I see her. Ask him."
gn.en.gn.obj-pron.title: Object pronouns
gn.en.gn.past-be.note: The past of be: I, he, she, and it take "was"; you, we, and they take "were". "I was at home. They were happy."
gn.en.gn.past-be.title: was / were
gn.en.gn.past-irreg-top25.note: The most common verbs change form in the past: go and went, have and had, see and saw, do and did, get and got, make and made.
gn.en.gn.past-irreg-top25.title: Irregular past (top verbs)
gn.en.gn.past-quest-neg.note: "Did you see it? I didn't go." Did carries the past, so the main verb returns to its base form.
gn.en.gn.past-quest-neg.title: did: questions & negatives
gn.en.gn.past-reg.note: Add -ed for finished actions: "I worked. She visited her mother." The same form works for every person.
gn.en.gn.past-reg.title: Past simple: -ed
gn.en.gn.plural-irreg.note: Some nouns change instead of adding -s: man and men, woman and women, child and children, person and people, foot and feet.
gn.en.gn.plural-irreg.title: Irregular plurals
gn.en.gn.plural-reg.note: Add -s for more than one, or -es after s, sh, ch, and x: one cat, two cats; one box, two boxes.
gn.en.gn.plural-reg.title: Regular plurals
gn.en.gn.poss-adj.note: My, your, his, her, its, our, their — put them before the noun: "her book", "our house", "their names".
gn.en.gn.poss-adj.title: Possessive adjectives
gn.en.gn.poss-s.note: Add 's to the owner: "Anna's dog", "my brother's car". English puts the owner first and the thing owned second.
gn.en.gn.poss-s.title: Possessive 's
gn.en.gn.prep-place.note: In, on, under, next to, behind, in front of, between — the little words that say where: "The keys are on the table."
gn.en.gn.prep-place.title: Prepositions of place
gn.en.gn.pres-cont.note: Be plus verb-ing for right now: "I am eating. They are working. Look, it is raining."
gn.en.gn.pres-cont.title: Present continuous
gn.en.gn.pres-simple-3sg.note: With he, she, and it, the verb takes -s: "She works. He watches." It is the most-forgotten letter in English, so give it extra care.
gn.en.gn.pres-simple-3sg.title: 3rd person -s
gn.en.gn.pres-simple-base.note: For habits and facts, use the base verb: "I work at home. They live in Lima." No ending changes for these subjects.
gn.en.gn.pres-simple-base.title: Present simple: I / you / we / they
gn.en.gn.pron-subject.note: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. English wants the subject said out loud in nearly every sentence — "am tired" needs its "I".
gn.en.gn.pron-subject.title: Subject pronouns
gn.en.gn.simple-vs-cont.note: "I drink coffee every day" is a habit; "I am drinking coffee" is this moment. The time words are your clue.
gn.en.gn.simple-vs-cont.title: Habit or right now?
gn.en.gn.some-any.note: "Some" in positive sentences ("I have some money") and "any" in negatives and questions ("Do you have any money?").
gn.en.gn.some-any.title: some / any
gn.en.gn.sv-order.note: English sentences go Subject–Verb–Object: "I eat apples." The order carries the meaning, so keep the doer first and the action second.
gn.en.gn.sv-order.title: Basic word order
gn.en.gn.there-is-are.note: To say something exists: "There is a bank. There are two cafes." Match is or are to how many things you mean.
gn.en.gn.there-is-are.title: there is / there are
gn.en.gn.time-prep.note: "At" for clock times (at five), "on" for days and dates (on Monday), "in" for months, years, and parts of the day (in May, in the morning).
gn.en.gn.time-prep.title: at / on / in for time
gn.en.gn.time-telling.note: Start with "It's": "It's three o'clock. It's half past two. It's seven fifteen." The "it" stays even though nothing is named.
gn.en.gn.time-telling.title: Telling the time
gn.en.gn.wh-quest-be.note: What, where, who, or how, then be, then the subject: "Where are you? What is this? Who is that?"
gn.en.gn.wh-quest-be.title: Wh-questions with be
gn.en.gn.would-like.note: "I'd like a coffee, please" is the polite way to order or ask for something — softer than "I want".
gn.en.gn.would-like.title: I'd like (polite)
ovl.es.en.a1.u10.note: False-friend patrol for work talk: actualmente is not "actually", asistir is not "assist", éxito is not "exit", and carpeta is not "carpet".
ovl.es.en.a1.u12.note: Adjectives go BEFORE the noun and don't take plural -s: "los coches rojos" becomes "the red cars", not "the cars reds".
ovl.es.en.a1.u24.note: "¿De quién es esto?" becomes one word: "Whose is this?" — whose does the whole "de quién" job.
ovl.es.en.gn.adv-freq.note: In Spanish these words roam ("Voy siempre", "Siempre voy"); English parks them before the main verb and after be: "I usually walk. She is often late."
ovl.es.en.gn.art-the.note: General statements drop "the" in English: "La vida es bella" is "Life is beautiful", and "me gustan los perros" is "I like dogs".
ovl.es.en.gn.articles-a-an.note: Un/una maps well onto a/an, but English adds one for professions: "Soy ingeniera" needs the article — "I am an engineer."
ovl.es.en.gn.be-1sg-2sg.note: Ser and estar both land on the same English verb: "be". Soy alta and estoy cansada are both "I am ..." — one verb does both jobs.
ovl.es.en.gn.be-all.note: Whether you'd pick ser or estar in Spanish, English uses one verb: "the shop is open" (estar sense) and "the shop is small" (ser sense) share the same "is".
ovl.es.en.gn.be-yesno-q.note: Spanish can ask with rising intonation alone ("¿Estás cansado?"); English moves be to the front: "Are you tired?" Intonation alone reads as a statement.
ovl.es.en.gn.can-ability.note: Saber (a learned skill) and poder (possibility or permission) both become "can": sé nadar and puedo ir are "I can swim" and "I can go".
ovl.es.en.gn.comp-superl.note: "Más grande que" becomes "-er than" for short adjectives (bigger than) and "more ... than" for long ones — the two-track split is the new part.
ovl.es.en.gn.dem-sg.note: Spanish has three distances (este, ese, aquel); English has two. Both ese and aquel usually land on "that".
ovl.es.en.gn.do-neg.note: "No veo nada" uses one negative in English: "I don't see anything" — don't plus a positive word, not a double negative.
ovl.es.en.gn.do-quest.note: Spanish questions work by intonation; English inserts do/does: "¿Te gusta el café?" becomes "Do you like coffee?"
ovl.es.en.gn.dummy-it.note: "Llueve" has no subject; English demands one: "IT is raining. IT's late. IT's cold." The it points at nothing — it just fills the seat.
ovl.es.en.gn.going-to.note: Positive transfer: "voy a viajar" maps word for word onto "I'm going to travel". Trust it — this one works exactly like Spanish.
ovl.es.en.gn.have-got.note: Watch the tener idioms: tengo hambre, sed, and 20 años all switch verbs in English — "I AM hungry", "I AM thirsty", "I AM 20".
ovl.es.en.gn.how-much-many.note: Cuánto/cuánta becomes "how much" and cuántos/cuántas becomes "how many" — English splits by countability instead of gender.
ovl.es.en.gn.imperatives.note: Spanish has separate tú/usted commands; English has one imperative for everyone. "Please" carries the courtesy that usted used to carry.
ovl.es.en.gn.like-want-noun.note: "Me gusta el té" flips: the liker becomes the subject in English — "I like tea." No "me" at the front, no article on general things.
ovl.es.en.gn.obj-pron.note: Spanish puts object pronouns before the verb ("te llamo"); English puts them after: "I'll call you. I see her. Ask him."
ovl.es.en.gn.past-be.note: Era, estaba, fue, and estuvo all collapse into was/were. English past-be is the simple one — don't hunt for the aspect split yet.
ovl.es.en.gn.past-reg.note: The -ed ending has three sounds: /t/ (worked), /d/ (played), /ɪd/ (visited). Say "visited" with three syllables, "worked" with one.
ovl.es.en.gn.plural-irreg.note: "La gente es..." is singular in Spanish, but "people" is plural in English: "people are friendly", not "people is".
ovl.es.en.gn.poss-adj.note: "Su" is ambiguous in Spanish; English splits it: his, her, its, and their are different words. Match the owner, not the thing owned.
ovl.es.en.gn.poss-s.note: Spanish has no 's: "el perro de Ana" turns around into "Ana's dog" — owner first, thing second.
ovl.es.en.gn.prep-place.note: Spanish "en" covers being inside, on top of, and at a place; English splits it into in, on, and at. "En la mesa" is usually "on the table".
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-cont.note: Estoy comiendo maps neatly onto "I am eating" — trust the pattern: be + verb-ing, with the -ing doing the job of -ando/-iendo.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-simple-3sg.note: Spanish conjugates every person, so the lone English -s feels invisible. It is the top A1 slip: "she work" needs its -s — "she works".
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-simple-base.note: Spanish packs the person into the ending (hablo, hablas); English keeps the verb bare and leans on the pronoun: I speak, you speak.
ovl.es.en.gn.pron-subject.note: Spanish drops subject pronouns ("Soy Ana"); English keeps them. Say "I am Ana" — the bare "am Ana" sounds broken to English ears.
ovl.es.en.gn.simple-vs-cont.note: Spanish "como" covers both; English splits them: "I eat" is the habit and "I am eating" is right now. Pick by the time words.
ovl.es.en.gn.some-any.note: Spanish often uses no word at all ("¿Tienes dinero?"); English likes "some" in positives and "any" in questions and negatives: "Do you have any money?"
ovl.es.en.gn.sv-order.note: Spanish lets you move words around ("Llegó María ayer"); English holds the Subject–Verb–Object line. Keep the doer first, even when it feels repetitive.
ovl.es.en.gn.there-is-are.note: "Hay" is one invariable word; English matches the number: there IS a cafe, there ARE two cafes.
ovl.es.en.gn.time-prep.note: Spanish "en" and "a" split three ways in English time phrases: at five, on Monday, in May. Learn the trio as one set.
ovl.es.en.gn.time-telling.note: "Son las tres" becomes "It's three o'clock" — English uses singular "it's" for every hour, plus o'clock on the hour.
ovl.es.en.gn.wh-quest-be.note: "¿De dónde eres?" becomes "Where are you from?" — the little word (from) moves to the end in everyday English questions.
ovl.es.en.gn.would-like.note: "Quisiera" and "me gustaría" both map onto "I'd like" — the same polite move works in cafés, shops, and hotels.

cando.en.a2.u01.interrupted: Can say what was happening when something else suddenly happened.
cando.en.a2.u01.ongoing: Can describe what they were doing at a specific moment in the past.
cando.en.a2.u02.habits: Can describe past habits and states that are no longer true.
cando.en.a2.u02.then-now: Can compare what things used to be like with how they are now.
cando.en.a2.u03.experiences: Can ask and talk about life experiences without saying when, and tell been from gone.
cando.en.a2.u04.duration: Can say how long something has been true, using for and since.
cando.en.a2.u04.progress: Can say what they have already done, still need to do, or have just finished.
cando.en.a2.u05.past-vs-perfect: Can choose past simple or present perfect depending on whether a time is finished, and can narrate a change and how it started.
cando.en.a2.u06.offers: Can offer to help or make a quick promise using will in the moment.
cando.en.a2.u06.predictions: Can make simple predictions with will, including a short weather forecast.
cando.en.a2.u07.arrangements: Can state a fixed arrangement with a time, using the present continuous.
cando.en.a2.u07.plans: Can talk about a plan already made, choosing going to over will.
cando.en.a2.u08.conditions: Can say what happens or will happen if a condition is met, using if with the present or with will.
cando.en.a2.u08.timing: Can link one future action to another with when or as soon as.
cando.en.a2.u09.advice: Can give simple advice about everyday problems, using should and shouldn't.
cando.en.a2.u10.rules: Can explain the rules of a place and say what is required, allowed, or forbidden, using have to, must, and mustn't.
cando.en.a2.u11.requests: Can make a polite request with could, and offer or ask for what they'd like with would.
cando.en.a2.u12.possibility: Can say what might or may happen or be true, without claiming it is certain.
cando.en.a2.u13.quantity-questions: Can ask how much something costs or how many there are, using how much and how many correctly.
cando.en.a2.u13.quantity-words: Can use many, much, and a lot of correctly with countable and uncountable nouns, and request simple quantities when shopping.
cando.en.a2.u14.amounts: Can say when something is too much, not quite enough, or just right, and ask for a small amount using a few or a little.
cando.en.a2.u15.equal: Can say whether two things are equal or not, using as … as and not as … as.
cando.en.a2.u15.manner: Can compare how well, fast, or often something is done, using comparative adverbs.
cando.en.a2.u16.feedback: Can describe how something was done and how well or badly it was done, using adverbs of manner and degree.
cando.en.a2.u17.gerunds: Can talk about likes and dislikes for free-time activities, using enjoy, like, love, hate, and stop before an -ing verb.
cando.en.a2.u18.goals: Can say what they want, need, hope, or have decided to do, using verb + to-infinitive.
cando.en.a2.u18.purpose: Can say why they did or are doing something, using to + verb for purpose.
cando.en.a2.u19.devices: Can explain how to use an everyday device, using phrasal verbs like turn on/off and get up, and verb + preposition pairs like listen to, wait for, and look for.
cando.en.a2.u20.identify: Can describe a person, place, or thing precisely by adding a defining detail with who, which, or that.
cando.en.a2.u21.possession: Can say what belongs to them and to others without repeating the noun, using mine, yours, his, hers, ours, and theirs.
cando.en.a2.u21.reflexive: Can say when the same person does and receives an action, using myself, yourself, and the other -self/-selves pronouns.
cando.en.a2.u22.opinions: Can give an opinion with a reason, add a result, and make a contrast, using because, so, and although.
cando.en.a2.u23.navigation: Can give and follow directions across town, using into, through, across, along, past, and over to show movement.
cando.en.a2.u24.events: Can ask and answer detailed questions about a recent event — who did something, what happened, and why — choosing the right word order for subject and object questions.
cando.en.a2.u25.celebrations: Can describe a celebration from their culture, compare it with others, and say what they enjoy about it.
cando.en.a2.u26.review: Can bring together what's happened, what's required, and what they enjoy doing in one account.
cando.en.a2.u27.my-year: Can give a short spoken and written account of their year: what happened, what has changed, and what comes next.
cando.en.a2.u28.show: Can put the whole of Arc 2 together in one review session.
cando.en.b1.u01.past-habits: Can describe past habits and routines that are no longer true, using used to and would.
cando.en.b1.u01.story: Can tell a story that weaves background details with the events that happened, in order.
cando.en.b1.u02.order: Can put two past events in order, marking which one happened first.
cando.en.b1.u02.what-had-happened: Can say what had already happened before noticing something.
cando.en.b1.u03.duration: Can say how long something has been going on, using for and since.
cando.en.b1.u03.result-or-activity: Can tell a finished result apart from an activity that might still be going on.
cando.en.b1.u04.articles: Can apply the finer article rules — the with a superlative or a one-of-a-kind thing, no article for meals and languages, a/an for jobs and rates.
cando.en.b1.u04.best-ever: Can rank an experience as the best or worst using a superlative with the present perfect and ever.
cando.en.b1.u05.future-in-progress: Can describe what they will be doing at a specific point in the future.
cando.en.b1.u05.suggestions-offers: Can make suggestions and offers with Shall we and Shall I.
cando.en.b1.u06.hypotheticals: Can imagine an unreal present or future with if plus a past form and would, and give a reason why.
cando.en.b1.u06.real-or-imagined: Can tell a real possibility from an imagined one, choosing between if with will and if with would.
cando.en.b1.u07.if-only: Can sharpen a wish into something more heartfelt using if only.
cando.en.b1.u07.wishes: Can express a wish about how things are now, using wish with a past form to show it isn't true.
cando.en.b1.u08.prepare-in-case: Can prepare for a possibility with in case, and state a condition with as long as.
cando.en.b1.u08.warn-unless: Can warn about an outcome that depends on a condition, using unless.
cando.en.b1.u09.deduction: Can weigh how certain something is and explain the evidence, using must, might, and can't be.
cando.en.b1.u10.obligation-past: Can say what they had to do in the past and what they will have to do in the future.
cando.en.b1.u10.permission-any-tense: Can talk about what was or wasn't allowed, in any tense.
cando.en.b1.u11.made-or-let: Can say what someone made or let them do, and what they make or let other people do.
cando.en.b1.u11.want-someone-to: Can say what they want, ask, tell, or expect another person to do.
cando.en.b1.u12.processes: Can explain how something is made, used, or produced, without needing to say who does it, using the present passive.
cando.en.b1.u13.built: Can describe when and how something was built, made, written, or discovered, using the past passive.
cando.en.b1.u13.passive-by: Can add the doer to a past passive sentence with by, only when that detail is the news.
cando.en.b1.u14.report-speech: Can report what someone said, stepping the tense back appropriately.
cando.en.b1.u14.say-or-tell: Can choose correctly between say and tell when reporting speech.
cando.en.b1.u15.reported-questions: Can report what someone asked, keeping yes/no questions with if or whether and wh-questions in flat statement order.
cando.en.b1.u15.reported-requests: Can report what someone told or asked them to do, using tell or ask plus an object and a to-infinitive.
cando.en.b1.u16.drop-relative: Can drop who, which, or that when it is the object of the added detail, as in "the neighborhood I love."
cando.en.b1.u16.where-whose: Can define a place by where it is or a person by whose something is, as in "the street where I live" and "a neighbor whose garden is full of flowers."
cando.en.b1.u17.verb-pattern-contrast: Can choose correctly between -ing and to after remember, stop, and try, and knows how the meaning changes.
cando.en.b1.u17.verb-pattern-more: Can use -ing after suggest, avoid, mind, and keep.
cando.en.b1.u18.phrasal-idioms: Can use common phrasal-verb pairs whose meaning isn't obvious from the parts — find out, give up, run out — to work through an everyday problem.
cando.en.b1.u18.phrasal-separable: Can place a pronoun in the middle of an everyday separable phrasal verb, like turn it on or put it away.
cando.en.b1.u19.linking: Can connect ideas across sentences with however, therefore, and instead to contrast or draw a conclusion.
cando.en.b1.u19.purpose: Can state purpose in a fuller way, using in order to and so that.
cando.en.b1.u20.echoes: Can agree with what someone said by echoing their verb with so or neither.
cando.en.b1.u20.tags: Can check or confirm something with a short question tag at the end.
cando.en.b1.u21.indefinites: Can talk about unspecified people, things, and places, using some-, any-, no-, and every- words correctly together.
cando.en.b1.u22.reactions: Can react to something watched or heard and explain why, choosing correctly between the -ed and -ing adjective forms.
cando.en.b1.u23.results: Can explain a result built into a description — too slow to catch it, so strong that it broke, such a close game — using too...to, so...that, and such a.
cando.en.b1.u24.indirect-questions: Can ask for information politely, softening the question with Could you tell me, Do you know, or I was wondering.
cando.en.b1.u25.pairs: Can say whether something is true of two people or things together, only one of them, or neither, using both, either, and neither.
cando.en.b1.u25.preferences: Can say which of two things they prefer, and ask others which they would rather have.
cando.en.b1.u26.work-life: Can talk about a job, a career, and colleagues, and can retell a job interview from both sides — answering questions and reporting what was asked and said.
cando.en.b1.u27.big-questions: Can take a stance on a big question, support it with a hypothetical and a reason, and connect the ideas with however/therefore and a deduction.
cando.en.b1.u28.review: Can bring together stories, hypothetical situations, what other people said, and their own opinions in one account.
cando.en.b1.u29.five-stories: Can give a short spoken and written portfolio: a past narrative with one past-perfect event, a hypothetical, a reported conversation, a passive process description, and an opinion with discourse connectors.
cando.en.b1.u30.show: Can put the whole of Arc 3 together in one review session.
gn.en.gn.adj-ed-ing.note: The -ing form describes what causes a feeling; the -ed form describes the feeling itself: "the film is boring, so I'm bored."
gn.en.gn.adj-ed-ing.title: -ed or -ing adjectives
gn.en.gn.adv-degree.note: Very, really, quite, and too sit before an adjective to turn it up or down: "really tired, quite good, too late."
gn.en.gn.adv-degree.title: Adverbs of degree
gn.en.gn.adv-manner.note: Add -ly to describe how an action happens: "She speaks slowly." A few keep their own shape — well, fast, hard.
gn.en.gn.adv-manner.title: Adverbs of manner
gn.en.gn.articles-deep.note: The marks something unique, a superlative, or a river; the zero article suits meals, languages, and most streets; a or an fits jobs and rates: "the fastest, breakfast, twice a day."
gn.en.gn.articles-deep.title: Articles: the finer rules
gn.en.gn.as-as.note: "As … as" marks two things as equal (as tall as me), and "not as … as" marks one as less: "It's not as cheap as before."
gn.en.gn.as-as.title: as … as
gn.en.gn.be-allowed-to.note: "Be allowed to" expresses permission in any tense: "We weren't allowed to talk in class. You're allowed to park here."
gn.en.gn.be-allowed-to.title: be allowed to
gn.en.gn.comp-adverbs.note: To compare how something is done, use more, -er, or an irregular form with than: "She types more quickly. He runs faster. They play better than us."
gn.en.gn.comp-adverbs.title: Comparative adverbs
gn.en.gn.cond-first-vs-second.note: The first conditional weighs a possible plan; the second imagines something unlikely: "If it rains, we'll stay in" against "If I won the lottery, I'd travel."
gn.en.gn.cond-first-vs-second.title: Real or imagined?
gn.en.gn.cond-first.note: If plus present, will, for a real future possibility: "If it rains, we'll stay in." The will stays out of the if-half.
gn.en.gn.cond-first.title: First conditional
gn.en.gn.cond-second.note: If plus a past form, then would plus a verb, imagines a present or future that isn't real: "If I had more time, I would travel."
gn.en.gn.cond-second.title: Second conditional
gn.en.gn.cond-zero.note: If plus present, present, for things that are generally true: "If you heat ice, it melts." Both halves stay in the present.
gn.en.gn.cond-zero.title: Zero conditional
gn.en.gn.conn-discourse.note: However, therefore, and instead link one sentence to the next: "It was late. However, we kept going."
gn.en.gn.conn-discourse.title: however / therefore / instead
gn.en.gn.could-past-polite.note: Could looks back at a past ability ("I could swim at five") and softens a request in the present ("Could you help me?").
gn.en.gn.could-past-polite.title: could
gn.en.gn.count-uncount.note: Some nouns — water, money, rice — are treated as a mass: no plural -s and no "a" in front. Others count one by one as usual.
gn.en.gn.count-uncount.title: Countable & uncountable
gn.en.gn.echo-so-neither.note: Agree by echoing the helper verb: "I love it." "So do I." Positive echoes take so, negative ones take neither.
gn.en.gn.echo-so-neither.title: So do I / Neither do I
gn.en.gn.few-little.note: A few goes with countable nouns and a little with uncountable ones; drop the "a" and few or little hints at not enough: "a few friends" against "few friends."
gn.en.gn.few-little.title: (a) few / (a) little
gn.en.gn.for-since.note: For measures a length of time (for two years); since names the point it started (since 2020). Both pair naturally with the present perfect.
gn.en.gn.for-since.title: for / since
gn.en.gn.future-cont.note: Will be plus -ing pictures an action in progress at a future moment: "This time tomorrow I'll be flying."
gn.en.gn.future-cont.title: Future continuous
gn.en.gn.gerund-after-verbs.note: After like, love, hate, enjoy, mind, and stop, the next verb takes -ing: "I enjoy cooking. Do you mind waiting?"
gn.en.gn.gerund-after-verbs.title: verb + -ing
gn.en.gn.had-to.note: Obligation shifts through time: "I had to wear a uniform" looks back, "You'll have to book early" looks ahead.
gn.en.gn.had-to.title: had to / will have to
gn.en.gn.have-to.note: Have to states an obligation; don't have to says there is none — not that something is forbidden: "I have to work" against "You don't have to come."
gn.en.gn.have-to.title: have to / don't have to
gn.en.gn.if-only.note: "If only" sharpens a wish into something more heartfelt: "If only it were warmer." It runs on the same past-form machinery as wish.
gn.en.gn.if-only.title: If only
gn.en.gn.in-case-as-long-as.note: In case prepares for a possibility ("take an umbrella in case it rains"); as long as sets a condition ("you can stay as long as you're quiet").
gn.en.gn.in-case-as-long-as.title: in case / as long as
gn.en.gn.in-order-to.note: "In order to" and "so that" spell out purpose in a fuller way: "in order to save time, so that everyone can hear."
gn.en.gn.in-order-to.title: in order to / so that
gn.en.gn.indef-pronouns.note: Combine some-, any-, no-, and every- with body, thing, and where, and follow the same some/any polarity: "someone called, but nobody answered."
gn.en.gn.indef-pronouns.title: somebody / anything / nowhere
gn.en.gn.indirect-questions.note: Inside a polite frame the inner question un-inverts: "Where is the station?" becomes "Could you tell me where the station is?"
gn.en.gn.indirect-questions.title: Could you tell me where…?
gn.en.gn.infinitive-after-verbs.note: After want, need, hope, decide, and would like, the next verb takes "to": "I want to go. She decided to stay."
gn.en.gn.infinitive-after-verbs.title: verb + to-infinitive
gn.en.gn.infinitive-purpose.note: "To + verb" answers why you did something: "I came to help." It carries the sense of "in order to."
gn.en.gn.infinitive-purpose.title: Infinitive of purpose
gn.en.gn.make-let.note: After make and let, the object is followed by a bare verb with no "to": "They made us wait. She let me drive."
gn.en.gn.make-let.title: make / let + bare verb
gn.en.gn.might-may.note: Might and may point to possibility rather than certainty: "It might rain. She may be late." Both leave the outcome open.
gn.en.gn.might-may.title: might / may
gn.en.gn.modal-deduction.note: Modals can weigh how sure you are: "It must be cold out. She can't be home yet. He might be busy." The verb reflects the evidence.
gn.en.gn.modal-deduction.title: must / might / can't be
gn.en.gn.much-many-alot.note: Many pairs with countable nouns, much with uncountable ones, and a lot of works comfortably with both: "many books, much time, a lot of either."
gn.en.gn.much-many-alot.title: much / many / a lot of
gn.en.gn.must-mustnt.note: Must marks a strong rule; mustn't marks a prohibition, which is a different idea from don't have to: "You mustn't park here."
gn.en.gn.must-mustnt.title: must / mustn't
gn.en.gn.narrative-tenses.note: A story weaves the past simple for events, the past continuous for background, and sequencers like first, then, and finally to move it along: "I was walking home when I saw her, so I stopped."
gn.en.gn.narrative-tenses.title: Telling a story in the past
gn.en.gn.passive-by.note: Name the doer with "by" only when that detail is the news: "It was painted by my sister." Otherwise the passive can leave it out.
gn.en.gn.passive-by.title: by + doer
gn.en.gn.passive-past.note: The past passive pairs was or were with a past participle: "The bridge was built in 1900. The letters were sent yesterday."
gn.en.gn.passive-past.title: Past passive
gn.en.gn.passive-present.note: Be plus a past participle shifts focus onto what happens rather than who does it: "Rice is grown here." The doer can stay unnamed.
gn.en.gn.passive-present.title: Present passive
gn.en.gn.past-cont.note: Use was or were plus an -ing verb for something in progress at a past moment: "I was cooking when you called." It sets the scene rather than reporting a finished event.
gn.en.gn.past-cont.title: Past continuous
gn.en.gn.past-perfect-vs-past.note: The past perfect marks the step that came first; after before, after, or by the time, the order is often clear enough on its own: "After she left, we ate."
gn.en.gn.past-perfect-vs-past.title: Order of past events
gn.en.gn.past-perfect.note: Had plus a past participle marks the earlier of two past events: "The train had left when I arrived." It steps one moment further back.
gn.en.gn.past-perfect.title: Past perfect
gn.en.gn.past-simple-vs-cont.note: A longer background action (was or were + -ing) is often cut short by a quick one in the past simple, joined by when or while: "I was reading when the lights went out."
gn.en.gn.past-simple-vs-cont.title: Interrupted past
gn.en.gn.perf-cont-vs-simple.note: "I've painted the room" points at the finished result; "I've been painting" points at the activity, which may still be going. One counts the outcome, the other the effort.
gn.en.gn.perf-cont-vs-simple.title: Result or duration?
gn.en.gn.phrasal-separable.note: Some phrasal verbs split around the object, and a pronoun sits in the middle: "turn the light on" or "turn it on."
gn.en.gn.phrasal-separable.title: Separable phrasal verbs
gn.en.gn.phrasal-verbs-1.note: A verb plus a small particle can shift the meaning: get up, turn on, look for, put on. The pair works as a single idea.
gn.en.gn.phrasal-verbs-1.title: Phrasal verbs I
gn.en.gn.phrasal-verbs-2.note: More everyday pairs — find out, give up, carry on, look after, run out of, sort out — carry meanings you can't guess from the parts.
gn.en.gn.phrasal-verbs-2.title: Phrasal verbs II
gn.en.gn.poss-pron.note: Mine, yours, his, hers, ours, and theirs stand alone with no noun after them: "That book is mine."
gn.en.gn.poss-pron.title: Possessive pronouns
gn.en.gn.prep-movement.note: Into, out of, through, across, along, past, and over describe direction of travel rather than a fixed place: "walk through the park, across the bridge."
gn.en.gn.prep-movement.title: Prepositions of movement
gn.en.gn.pres-cont-future.note: The present continuous can point to a fixed arrangement with a set time: "I'm meeting Ana at six." The time word keeps it from sounding like right now.
gn.en.gn.pres-cont-future.title: Present continuous for arrangements
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-been-gone.note: "Has been to" means went and came back; "has gone to" means still there: "She has been to Paris" against "She has gone to Paris."
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-been-gone.title: been vs gone
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-cont.note: Have or has been plus -ing describes an action still running or just stopped: "I've been waiting for an hour." It leans on the length of the activity.
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-cont.title: Present perfect continuous
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-exp.note: Have or has plus a past participle talks about life experience without saying when: "I have visited Rome." The moment is not the point — the experience is.
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-exp.title: Present perfect: experience
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-vs-past.note: A finished time word (yesterday, last week) calls for the past simple; an unfinished or unstated time leans on the present perfect. "I saw it yesterday" but "I have seen it."
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-vs-past.title: Present perfect vs past simple
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-yet-already.note: Already marks something done sooner than expected, yet asks or denies in questions and negatives, and just points to the very recent past: "I've just eaten. Have you finished yet?"
gn.en.gn.pres-perf-yet-already.title: already / yet / just
gn.en.gn.question-tags.note: A tag mirrors the helper verb and flips its sign: "It's cold, isn't it? You don't mind, do you?"
gn.en.gn.question-tags.title: Question tags
gn.en.gn.question-words-deep.note: When the question word is the subject, skip do: "Who called you?" When it's the object, keep it: "Who did you call?" Compare "What happened?"
gn.en.gn.question-words-deep.title: Subject vs object questions
gn.en.gn.reflexive.note: When the subject and object are the same, use myself, yourself, herself, and the rest: "I hurt myself. Help yourselves."
gn.en.gn.reflexive.title: Reflexive pronouns
gn.en.gn.rel-object-omit.note: When the relative word is the object, English lets you drop it: "the film we watched" works as well as "the film that we watched."
gn.en.gn.rel-object-omit.title: Dropping the relative
gn.en.gn.rel-where-whose.note: Where points to a place and whose to a possessor: "the town where I grew up, the writer whose book won."
gn.en.gn.rel-where-whose.title: Relatives: where / whose
gn.en.gn.rel-who-which.note: Use who for people and which or that for things to add essential detail: "the man who lives here, the bag that fits."
gn.en.gn.rel-who-which.title: Relative clauses (defining)
gn.en.gn.reported-commands.note: Report a request or order with tell or ask plus an object and a to-infinitive: "She told me to wait. He asked us not to call."
gn.en.gn.reported-commands.title: Reported requests & commands
gn.en.gn.reported-questions.note: Reported questions drop the question word order and read like statements: "Where do you live?" becomes "He asked where I lived." Use if or whether for yes-no ones.
gn.en.gn.reported-questions.title: Reported questions
gn.en.gn.reported-statements.note: To report what someone said, step the tense back one notch: "I'm tired" becomes "She said (that) she was tired."
gn.en.gn.reported-statements.title: Reported speech: statements
gn.en.gn.say-vs-tell.note: Tell wants a person right after it (tell me); say does not (say that…): "She told me the news" but "She said the news was good."
gn.en.gn.say-vs-tell.title: say / tell
gn.en.gn.shall-suggest.note: Shall with I or we offers or suggests: "Shall we start? Shall I open the window?"
gn.en.gn.shall-suggest.title: Shall we…?
gn.en.gn.should-advice.note: Should and shouldn't offer advice or an opinion, followed by a bare verb: "You should rest. You shouldn't skip breakfast."
gn.en.gn.should-advice.title: should / shouldn't
gn.en.gn.so-because-although.note: So introduces a result, because a reason, and although a contrast: "It was late, so we left. We stayed because it was warm, although it rained."
gn.en.gn.so-because-although.title: so / because / although
gn.en.gn.superl-perf-ever.note: A superlative teams up with the present perfect and ever to rank an experience: "It's the best film I have ever seen."
gn.en.gn.superl-perf-ever.title: The best I've ever…
gn.en.gn.time-clauses.note: After when, as soon as, before, or after, English uses a present tense for future meaning: "When I arrive, I'll call you" — not "when I will arrive."
gn.en.gn.time-clauses.title: Future time clauses
gn.en.gn.too-enough.note: Too before an adjective says more than you want (too hot); enough comes after an adjective but before a noun (warm enough, enough time).
gn.en.gn.too-enough.title: too / enough
gn.en.gn.too-to-so-that.note: "Too … to" and "so … that" build a result into the adjective: "too tired to drive, so tired that I slept."
gn.en.gn.too-to-so-that.title: too…to / so…that
gn.en.gn.unless.note: Unless means if…not: "We'll miss it unless we leave now." One word carries the whole negative condition.
gn.en.gn.unless.title: unless
gn.en.gn.used-to-vs-would.note: Both used to and would replay repeated past actions: "We would swim every summer." For past states, though, used to carries them and would does not.
gn.en.gn.used-to-vs-would.title: used to / would (past habits)
gn.en.gn.used-to.note: "Used to" describes a past habit or state that no longer holds: "I used to live in Lima." The verb after it stays bare — used to live, not used to lived.
gn.en.gn.used-to.title: used to
gn.en.gn.verb-obj-inf.note: Verbs like want, ask, tell, and expect take an object and then a to-infinitive: "I want you to listen. She asked me to wait."
gn.en.gn.verb-obj-inf.title: want someone to do
gn.en.gn.verb-patterns-contrast.note: With remember, stop, and try, the pattern changes the meaning: "stop smoking" (quit) against "stop to smoke" (pause in order to).
gn.en.gn.verb-patterns-contrast.title: remember / stop / try + -ing or to
gn.en.gn.verb-patterns-more.note: Suggest, avoid, mind, and keep all take -ing: "I suggest leaving early. Keep trying. I don't mind waiting."
gn.en.gn.verb-patterns-more.title: suggest / avoid / mind / keep
gn.en.gn.verb-prep-collocations.note: Certain verbs travel with a fixed preposition: listen to, wait for, look at, depend on. The pairing is worth learning whole.
gn.en.gn.verb-prep-collocations.title: verb + preposition
gn.en.gn.will-decide-offer.note: Reach for will when you decide, offer, or promise as you speak: "I'll help you. I'll get it." The choice is made in the moment.
gn.en.gn.will-decide-offer.title: will (decisions & offers)
gn.en.gn.will-predict.note: Will plus a bare verb states a prediction or a fact about the future: "It will rain later." The form stays the same from person to person.
gn.en.gn.will-predict.title: will (predictions)
gn.en.gn.will-vs-going-to.note: Going to fits a plan already in mind or evidence you can see; will fits a prediction or an on-the-spot decision: "We're going to paint" against "I'll paint it."
gn.en.gn.will-vs-going-to.title: will vs going to
gn.en.gn.wish-past.note: Wishes about the present use past forms: "I wish I had a garden. I wish I could stay." The past shape signals it isn't so.
gn.en.gn.wish-past.title: wish + past
gn.en.gn.would-like-offers.note: "Would you like…?" offers politely and "I'd like…" asks for something gently: "Would you like a coffee? I'd like to book a table."
gn.en.gn.would-like-offers.title: would you like…?
ovl.es.en.a2.u18.note: False-friend watch as you talk about goals: pretender is not "pretend" — it means to intend or aim — and intentar is simply "try."
ovl.es.en.a2.u22.note: In an opinion, mind discutir: it often means to argue, not only to discuss. Use discuss for a calm exchange, argue for a heated one.
ovl.es.en.b1.u03.note: Health false friends: constipado is a cold (not constipated), molestar is to bother (not molest), and embarazada means pregnant (not embarrassed).
ovl.es.en.b1.u22.note: Reaction-talk false friends: argumento is the plot (not an argument), un suceso is an event (not success), and sensible means sensitive (not sensible).
ovl.es.en.b1.u26.note: Work-talk false friends: realizar is "carry out" (not realize), soportar is "put up with" (not support), una solicitud is a job application, and compromiso is a commitment (not compromise).
ovl.es.en.gn.adj-ed-ing.note: Spanish "aburrido" covers both sides; English splits them: the -ing form names the cause, the -ed form names the feeling.
ovl.es.en.gn.articles-deep.note: Spanish keeps the article with languages and general nouns; English drops it: "el inglés es útil" becomes "English is useful."
ovl.es.en.gn.as-as.note: "Tan alto como" maps straight onto "as tall as" — the two "as" words frame the adjective.
ovl.es.en.gn.be-allowed-to.note: "No me dejaban salir" becomes "I wasn't allowed to go out" — be allowed to carries permission across the tenses.
ovl.es.en.gn.cond-first.note: "Si llueve, nos quedaremos" becomes "if it rains, we'll stay in." Keep the will out of the if-half — English does not put it there.
ovl.es.en.gn.cond-second.note: "Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría" becomes "if I had time, I would travel" — if plus past, then would. The would does not enter the if-half.
ovl.es.en.gn.cond-zero.note: This one transfers directly: "si calientas el hielo, se derrite" is "if you heat ice, it melts." Both halves stay in the present, just as in Spanish.
ovl.es.en.gn.conn-discourse.note: Sin embargo and por lo tanto become however and therefore, each followed by a comma: "It was late. However, we kept going."
ovl.es.en.gn.could-past-polite.note: Poder splits in English: past ability and a polite request both become could. "Podía nadar" is "I could swim"; "podrías ayudar" is "could you help?"
ovl.es.en.gn.count-uncount.note: Several nouns that count in Spanish do not in English: information, furniture, money, bread, and advice take no plural and no "a." "Un consejo" is "a piece of advice."
ovl.es.en.gn.echo-so-neither.note: "Yo también" and "yo tampoco" become echoes that match the helper verb: "So am I", "Neither can I" — not a flat "me too."
ovl.es.en.gn.few-little.note: "Poco/pocos" becomes little or few; mind the "a": a little and a few mean some, while little and few hint at not enough.
ovl.es.en.gn.for-since.note: "Desde hace" and "desde" both hide inside English: for measures the length (for two years), since marks the start (since 2020).
ovl.es.en.gn.future-cont.note: "I'll be flying" is ordinary speech in English, not something formal. Reach for it freely to place an action inside a future moment.
ovl.es.en.gn.gerund-after-verbs.note: After enjoy and mind, English wants -ing where Spanish uses the infinitive: "me gusta cocinar" becomes "I like cooking."
ovl.es.en.gn.had-to.note: As with other past questions, did carries the tense: "did you have to wait?", while the statement is "I had to wait."
ovl.es.en.gn.have-to.note: "No tienes que venir" means there is no obligation, not that it's forbidden: "you don't have to come." Read it as freedom, not a prohibition.
ovl.es.en.gn.in-case-as-long-as.note: "Por si acaso" becomes in case plus a present verb, and "siempre que" becomes as long as: "take it in case it rains; stay as long as you like."
ovl.es.en.gn.indef-pronouns.note: English keeps a single negative: "no vi a nadie" becomes "I didn't see anybody", not "didn't see nobody."
ovl.es.en.gn.indirect-questions.note: Inside a polite frame the question un-inverts — the classic Spanish-to-English slip: "could you tell me where the station is?", not "where is the station?"
ovl.es.en.gn.infinitive-after-verbs.note: "Quiero ir" becomes "I want to go" — the "to" is not optional in English, even though Spanish joins the verbs directly.
ovl.es.en.gn.infinitive-purpose.note: "Para + infinitivo" becomes "to + verb", not "for + -ing": "para aprender" is "to learn", not "for learning."
ovl.es.en.gn.make-let.note: Make and let take an object and then a bare verb — no "to": "me hicieron esperar" is "they made me wait", not "made me to wait."
ovl.es.en.gn.might-may.note: "Puede que llueva" and "a lo mejor" become might or may — pure uncertainty, not the ability sense of poder.
ovl.es.en.gn.modal-deduction.note: "Debe de estar cansado" becomes "he must be tired." For the negative guess, English uses can't be, not mustn't be.
ovl.es.en.gn.much-many-alot.note: Spanish "mucho/muchos" is one idea; English splits it into much and many, and a lot of covers both in positive sentences.
ovl.es.en.gn.must-mustnt.note: "No debes" lines up with mustn't, a prohibition — which is not the same as don't have to. The verb deber blurs the two, so keep them apart.
ovl.es.en.gn.narrative-tenses.note: This is the preterite/imperfect split you already own: events go into the past simple, background into the past continuous. The instinct from Spanish carries over.
ovl.es.en.gn.passive-past.note: "Fue construido en 1900" becomes "was built in 1900" — a straightforward, positive transfer.
ovl.es.en.gn.passive-present.note: Spanish prefers the se-passive; English uses be plus a participle: "se habla español" becomes "Spanish is spoken."
ovl.es.en.gn.past-cont.note: Estaba comiendo maps straight onto "I was eating" — the -ing quietly does the work of -ando/-iendo. Trust the pattern: was or were, then the -ing verb.
ovl.es.en.gn.past-perfect.note: "Había comido" becomes "had eaten" — a clean, positive transfer. Had plus the participle works just as the pluscuamperfecto does.
ovl.es.en.gn.past-simple-vs-cont.note: Spanish splits this with the imperfect and preterite; English splits it with was -ing against -ed. The action that gets interrupted takes was -ing: "I was cooking when he arrived."
ovl.es.en.gn.perf-cont-vs-simple.note: Spanish doesn't ask you to choose between result and activity, but English does: "I've painted it" against "I've been painting."
ovl.es.en.gn.phrasal-separable.note: Spanish has no real counterpart, so lean on the pattern: it's "turn it on", not "turn on it", with the pronoun in the middle.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-cont-future.note: "Quedo con Ana a las seis" becomes "I'm meeting Ana at six" — the present continuous, plus a time, carries the arrangement.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-perf-been-gone.note: Ha ido and ha estado split cleanly in English: gone means still away, been means went and came back. "Ha ido a Lima" is "has gone to Lima."
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-perf-cont.note: "Llevo dos años viviendo aquí" becomes "I have been living here for two years" — English has no llevar, so it leans on have been -ing.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-perf-exp.note: It resembles "he visitado", but English will not accept the present perfect with a finished time. "I have eaten at two" is wrong; once you name the time, switch to the past simple.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-perf-vs-past.note: This is the top A2 slip: "hoy he comido" is natural in Spanish, but "I have eaten at two" is not. Once the time is finished — even "today at two" — English wants the past simple.
ovl.es.en.gn.pres-perf-yet-already.note: Spanish "ya" turns into already or yet depending on polarity — already in positives, yet in questions and negatives. "Acabo de comer" becomes "I have just eaten."
ovl.es.en.gn.question-tags.note: Spanish "¿no?" and "¿verdad?" stay fixed; English tags mirror the helper and flip its sign. This is the hardest B1 habit to build, so it rewards steady practice.
ovl.es.en.gn.rel-object-omit.note: Spanish keeps que, but English drops the object relative freely: "the film we watched" needs no "that."
ovl.es.en.gn.rel-where-whose.note: Cuyo is fading from spoken Spanish, but whose is still required in English: "the writer whose book won."
ovl.es.en.gn.reported-commands.note: "Me dijo que esperara" becomes "she told me to wait" — the subjunctive request turns into tell or ask plus a to-infinitive.
ovl.es.en.gn.reported-questions.note: Keeping the question word order is the classic error: it's "she asked where I lived", not "asked where did I live."
ovl.es.en.gn.reported-statements.note: The backshift works much as it does in Spanish; the real trap is word order, which stays flat and statement-like in English.
ovl.es.en.gn.say-vs-tell.note: Decir covers both, but English splits them: tell needs a person (tell me), say does not. And you "explain to me", not "explain me."
ovl.es.en.gn.should-advice.note: "Deberías descansar" becomes "you should rest" — should plus a bare verb, with no "to" after it.
ovl.es.en.gn.so-because-although.note: Como, porque, and aunque map onto so, because, and although. Watch that because is not "because of", and English does not double "aunque…pero" — pick one.
ovl.es.en.gn.superl-perf-ever.note: English adds a word Spanish leaves out — "ever": "la mejor que he visto" becomes "the best I have ever seen."
ovl.es.en.gn.time-clauses.note: "Cuando llegue" uses the subjunctive; English simply uses the present: "when I arrive." The future "when I will arrive" is not how English says it.
ovl.es.en.gn.too-enough.note: "Demasiado" is too and "suficiente" is enough — but enough comes after an adjective and before a noun: "warm enough, enough time."
ovl.es.en.gn.too-to-so-that.note: "Demasiado cansado para conducir" becomes "too tired to drive", and "tan cansado que dormí" becomes "so tired that I slept."
ovl.es.en.gn.unless.note: "A menos que salgamos" uses the subjunctive; English uses a plain present after unless: "unless we leave."
ovl.es.en.gn.used-to-vs-would.note: The imperfect covers both in Spanish; English divides the work. Use used to for past states, and reserve would for repeated actions.
ovl.es.en.gn.used-to.note: Solía and the imperfect of habit land on "used to" plus a bare verb: "solía correr" becomes "I used to run" — used to run, not used to ran.
ovl.es.en.gn.verb-obj-inf.note: "Quiero que vengas" becomes "I want you to come" — the Spanish subjunctive turns into an object plus an infinitive in English.
ovl.es.en.gn.verb-patterns-contrast.note: "Dejar de fumar" becomes "stop smoking", while "acordarse de hacer" becomes "remember to do" — the pattern carries the meaning.
ovl.es.en.gn.will-decide-offer.note: Spanish offers with the present ("te ayudo"); English reaches for will at the moment of deciding: "I'll help you."
ovl.es.en.gn.will-predict.note: Both "lloverá" and "va a llover" exist in Spanish; in English, will does not change shape. One form — will rain — covers every person.
ovl.es.en.gn.will-vs-going-to.note: "Voy a" is going to; a decision made on the spot switches to will. English asks for a choice here that Spanish leaves open.
ovl.es.en.gn.wish-past.note: "Ojalá tuviera un jardín" becomes "I wish I had a garden." The past form after wish is what marks it as unreal.
ovl.es.en.gn.would-like-offers.note: "¿Quieres un café?" can sound blunt in English; "Would you like a coffee?" is the polite move. "Quisiera" becomes "I'd like."
